definition: Tex is the direct, metric unit of linear density for fibers and yarns: the mass in grams of 1,000 meters of material, with decitex (dtex) giving grams per 10,000 meters.
explanation: Tex belongs to a direct numbering system, so a larger number means a heavier, coarser strand for the same length. The same unit is intended for every stage and fiber type, from single fibers through slivers, rovings, tops, singles and plied yarns, cords and threads. Decimal prefixes keep the numbers convenient: decitex is common for filaments and staple fibers, while kilotex suits heavy slivers. Because tex, decitex and denier are all mass per length, they convert by fixed factors and never require knowledge of the fiber's density or cross-section.
example: A mill lists a polyester staple as 1.7 dtex and a finished yarn as 20 tex. The fiber figure describes individual fibers; the yarn figure describes the whole twisted strand. Converting, 1.7 dtex is about 1.5 denier, and 20 tex equals 200 dtex or 180 denier. Keeping track of which object each number describes prevents a buyer from comparing a fiber specification with a yarn specification.
caution: Tex is not diameter. Two yarns of equal tex can differ in thickness because polymer density, fiber packing, twist and bulking all change how much space a given mass occupies. A plied yarn's resultant tex also differs slightly from the simple sum of its singles because twisting shortens the components. Always check whether a figure refers to a fiber, a singles yarn or a finished plied yarn.
deeper: Linear density in tex is mass divided by length, expressed as grams per kilometer. Useful identities follow directly from the unit definitions: 1 tex equals 10 dtex, 1,000 millitex and 9 denier, so dtex is about 1.11 times the denier value. Tex converts to indirect counts by division: English cotton count Ne is about 590.5 divided by tex, and metric count Nm is 1,000 divided by tex. ASTM D861 sets out practice for designating linear density in tex, and ISO 1144 specifies the universal Tex System with recommended multiples and submultiples. Conversion tables replacing traditional counts with rounded tex values appear in ISO 2947 and ASTM D2260. In laboratory work, yarn linear density is found by weighing measured skeins after conditioning, since moisture content changes mass.
origins: Before tex, each branch of the trade used its own count: cotton hanks, worsted hanks, woollen runs, linen leas and silk or filament deniers. ISO Technical Committee 38 on Textiles worked on a single metric replacement in the 1950s, and A. G. Scroggie described the Tex universal yarn numbering system in Textile Research Journal in 1958. ISO later published the system as ISO 1144, with a 1973 edition and a current 2016 edition, alongside the ISO 2947 integrated conversion table of 1973.

definition: A 1958 US federal statute, 15 U.S.C. 70 et seq., requiring fiber content, country of origin and responsible-company disclosures for most textile fiber products sold in the United States.
explanation: The Act makes it unlawful to misbrand or falsely advertise textile fiber products in commerce. Covered products must carry a label stating the generic names of the constituent fibers and their percentages by weight, the name or registered identification number of the manufacturer or another responsible US company, and the country where the product was processed or manufactured. The Federal Trade Commission enforces the Act through its rules at 16 CFR Part 303, which define terms, list generic names, set content tolerances and describe how and where labels appear. Invoices and advertising are covered as well as labels.
example: A small importer brings in knitted throws that carry only a brand logo. Under the Act's framework, a compliance reviewer would ask descriptive questions: does a label state the generic fibers and percentages, identify a responsible company, and name the country of origin, and do the website listing and the invoices say the same thing? This is an illustration of what the rules cover, not advice about any real product.
caution: The Act governs disclosure of fiber identity and origin, not quality, safety or environmental performance. Products containing wool are handled under the separate Wool Products Labeling Act, and the statute and rules exempt or relax requirements for various listed items. Care instructions come from a different FTC rule, and flammability is governed by yet another statute, so identify which instrument actually answers the question being asked.
deeper: The statute is short and its sections map onto functions: 15 U.S.C. 70 contains definitions, 70a prohibits misbranding and false advertising in commerce, 70b sets out when a product is misbranded or falsely advertised (including the required label contents), 70c restricts removing required labels before sale, 70d requires records, and 70e provides for enforcement, with violations treated as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act. Percentages are by weight of the fiber content, and fibers present at less than 5 percent may generally be grouped as 'other fiber' unless the rules require them to be named, for example where the fiber has a clearly established functional significance. Checking a label means laboratory work: qualitative identification by microscopy, burning behavior, solubility or infrared spectroscopy, then quantitative analysis, often by selectively dissolving one component, compared against the tolerances in Part 303.
origins: Congress approved the Act on 2 September 1958 and it came into force in 1960. It extended to textiles generally the disclosure approach already applied to wool by the Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939, at a time when manufactured fibers sold under brand names were spreading through the consumer market. The FTC's Part 303 rules have been amended repeatedly, including a final rule published in February 2020, and now incorporate generic names from ISO 2076.
